summary: An April 1st joke RFC that purports to establish a Protocol Police, a body to assess and enforce correct protocol behavior. It plays on the IETF saying We are not the Protocol Police. It is humorous and not a real standard or organization.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC satirizes the idea of enforcing protocol rules. It pretends to establish a secret Protocol Police and describes absurd procedures and punishments.

subtitle: An April 1st satire pretends to establish a body that enforces protocol behavior.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke plays on the IETF saying, "We are not the Protocol Police," when discussing non-compliant implementations.
tldr.mechanism: It satirically describes a secret body, punishable offenses, reporting procedures and traffic-based punishments.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational humor document; the text's proposed Protocol Police are part of the satire.

today: RFC 8962 is an Informational April 1st joke document. Its Protocol Police are presented as satire.

sections.title: The Pretend Protocol Police
sections.content:
RFC 8962 is an April 1st satire built around the IETF saying, "We are not the Protocol Police." It pretends that the IETF has established a body to assess and enforce correct protocol behavior.

The document says the proposed body would enforce IETF standards and best practices. Its members would be selected by the IETF Nominating Committee but would not be publicly named.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st document takes the phrase Protocol Police literally. It pretends that a secret enforcement body has been created.

sections.title: Offenses, Reports and Punishments
sections.content:
The RFC lists protocol-layer violations, deliberate non-interoperability and disobeying RFCs as offenses. It says reports should be sent to /dev/null.

Its proposed punishments include a list of hosts whose packets other networks would drop and TCP RSTs for networks identified through Heuristic Internet Policing. These are satirical descriptions, not a real enforcement procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke lists offenses and punishments, including sending reports to /dev/null. The described enforcement is part of the satire.

sections.title: Satirical Oversight and Security
sections.content:
The RFC includes morality, security, privacy and human-rights sections. Its oversight section says the Protocol Police promise to overlook all activities, playing on the difference between overseeing and overlooking.

The security section claims there was no security before the Police arrived, and the conclusion says, "Case closed." These lines use mock-authoritative language for comic effect.
sections.plainLanguage: The oversight and security sections continue the satire through wordplay and exaggerated claims. The document ends with the phrase Case closed.
